💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept.
  • Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.
  • Sources indicate that sources remarked Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who at the moment serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept. 23. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.

Sources indicate that sources remarked Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who at the moment serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget. The White House submitted ethics paperwork on Ueland — required for nominations — to the GAO, according to a source.

Industry observers note that senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., on Thursday posted notice of a committee hearing Nov. 19 to examine more than a dozen presidential nominees for executive and judicial offices, including “a nominee to be Comptroller General.”.

Sources indicate that the post identifies by name all of the nominees except the candidate for comptroller general. The post has been filled by an acting comptroller general, Orice Williams Brown, since Gene L. Dodaro completed his 15-year term at the end of last year.

Industry observers note that the move by Paul to short-circuit the convening of a legislative commission to recommend candidates infuriated top Democrats, who excoriated the chairman in a joint statement Wednesday night. A special bipartisan, bicameral legislative commission is supposed to recommend at least three candidates for comptroller general to the president, according to statute.

Recent findings suggest that homeland Security Committee GOP staff solicited recommendations for a comptroller general from some Democratic congressional offices Wednesday afternoon, imposing a deadline of 8 a.m. Thursday, according to Democratic aides.

The president nominates the head of the GAO, the investigative arm of Congress, with the advice and consent of the Senate.

Recent findings suggest that paul pushed back on the criticism Thursday, saying, “Democrats have known about this for months and months and months.” He said the last time the special commission made recommendations for the office, when Barack Obama was president, “Democrats submitted their own list, Republicans submitted their own list. So they can complain all they want but they just need to make their list and submit it.”.

In the past, however, the special commission convened, sought applications for the position, interviewed candidates and deliberated before sending recommendations to the president.

A 1980 law states that when there is a vacancy in the comptroller general position, “there is established a commission to recommend individuals to the President for appointment to the vacant office,” and that the commission must submit at least three names.

Under the statute, the commission includes the speaker, Senate majority and minority leaders, House majority and minority leaders, chairs and ranking members of the Senate Homeland Security and House Oversight and Government Reform committees, and the Senate president pro tempore.

Sources indicate that in 1981, for example, after the law took effect, the two congressional leaders, Speaker Thomas P. “Tip” O’Neill Jr., D-Mass., and Senate Majority Leader Howard H. Baker, R-Tenn., sent a letter to President Ronald Reagan saying the special commission had met and voted to recommend eight candidates to succeed Comptroller General Elmer Staats.

“The members of the Commission have taken their statutory responsibility seriously,” they wrote.

In a recent development, reagan nominated Charles A. Bowsher, who was on the list, and he was confirmed.

After Bowsher’s term ended in 1996, the commission eventually formed, interviewed multiple candidates, and deliberated for several months. Republicans controlled both chambers, and Bill Clinton was president. The members of the commission could not reach agreement, and as a result, the Republicans on the committee submitted their list to Clinton, and the Democrats on the panel submitted theirs.

Clinton also had his own list. Clinton nominated David M. Walker, who was on all three lists, and he was confirmed by the Senate more than two years after Bowsher’s departure. Walker argued Thursday against short-circuiting the commission process.

“The position is of critical importance and the related statutory Commission process should not be circumvented," Walker remarked. "Doing so would undercut the credibility of the person and the effectiveness of the GAO.”.

Walker resigned in March of 2008, when George W. Bush was still president. He appointed Dodaro as acting comptroller general when he left. The commission got going several months later, creating a website with application instructions and candidate questions.

Over the next two years, the commission interviewed some 20 candidates. Democrats and Republicans on the panel were unable to reach agreement, and Democrats, who had a majority on the commission, submitted their own list to Obama in 2010. Republicans followed up with their list.

“The Commission has been working in earnest on this undertaking for more than one year and has dedicated considerable time and effort to present you with highly qualified candidates for this important position,” then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., along with other Democratic leaders, wrote to Obama when they submitted the Democrats’ list.

According to recent reports, the Democrats’ move drew a rebuke from Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who was ranking member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee at the time.

According to recent reports, collins mentioned in a statement she was “extremely disappointed” that Democrats “abruptly ended the selection process for the next Comptroller General without a bipartisan agreement” on the recommendations. “We have had several exceptionally qualified individuals apply to be the next leader of the GAO, and it should have been possible to come up with a consensus list.”.

Obama nominated and the Senate confirmed Dodaro, who was one of four recommendations from the Democrats.

Tired of using loud and unsightly window air conditioners or clunky and underpowered portable air conditioners? Even if you don’t have the means to install a fully ducted HVAC system in your home, you can still upgrade to a more powerful cooling system with a ductless air conditioner.

Ductless air conditioners, often called mini-splits, cool targeted areas of your home without relying on the ductwork. Instead, they connect a compact outdoor condenser to one or more indoor air handlers, which are usually mounted on a wall or ceiling.

To help narrow down the best ductless air conditioners, I compared models across capacity, efficiency, installation requirements, noise level, smart features, and overall value. I also spoke with HVAC expert Kim Lincoln, who has 25 years of industry experience, for guidance on how mini-splits work, when they make sense, and what shoppers should know before buying.

Many come with features like programmability, dehumidification settings, and, in a few instances, smartphone functionality.

As an added perk, most of these contraptions also double as heaters—which is useful during cooler months. I leaned on my experience with different types of cooling units, as well as product specs I reviewed during my research. The final list below represents the best in each category, including best budget and best for DIY installation.

I asked her a variety of questions about mini-splits, touching on topics like the differences between this type of air conditioner from other units, installation, and more. I also updated the products I recommend to reflect recent advances in smart home technology and energy efficiency.

Compared to window or portable air conditioners, ductless systems are more permanent, more powerful, and typically quieter. They also give you more control over specific rooms, so you can cool the spaces you actually use instead of the whole house at once. There are some drawbacks, though.

It has been revealed that ductless ACs run pricey (even setting aside the cost of installation). They’re also more visible than central air vents, and you need to size and place them carefully to cool a room evenly. DIY installs or wrong-sized units can cause problems in the long run.

Maintenance can also be difficult, as not all HVAC professionals are familiar with these products. However, for an older home with radiator heat (like mine is), it’s the best way to add efficient air conditioning without blocking most of our windows.

Recent findings suggest that first, decide how many indoor units you need and where you’ll place them. Unlike window units, mini-split systems are permanent fixtures, so carefully consider where they’ll be most efficient within your home.

It has been revealed that generally, a single ductless air conditioner can handle cooling a targeted area or a single room. If you’re cooling down multiple rooms, consider a multi-zone system so that you get even temperatures throughout your home.

It’s also essential to select a unit that’s powerful enough for the room it’s in—too small and it may not cool your space. The cooling capacity of air conditioners is typically measured in British Thermal Units, or BTUs, per hour.

According to recent reports, as a general rule of thumb, choose a unit that delivers 20 BTUs per square foot of living space. So, a 200-square-foot room needs at least a 4,000-BTU air conditioner. Those sensitive to noise should consider units with a quiet mode feature.

It has been revealed that it’s also notable to consider the electrical system in the area you initiative to install the mini-split. Many larger mini-splits require 208- to 230-volt power, which works with both commercial 208V electrical service and the 240V circuits typically used for major appliances in homes, while smaller systems may run on standard 120V outlets without any needed upgrades.

Quieter units are more desirable for bedrooms, living rooms, and nurseries, where a peaceful environment is essential. Look for ductless air conditioners with noise levels between 19 and 30 decibels, since this range can be compared to the sound of leaves rustling or a soft whisper.

Units with levels between 30 to 40 decibels are still suitable for other areas of the home, since this range is comparable to background noise or casual conversation.

While shopping for your ductless air conditioner, you may see “SEER” with a number next to it. SEER stands for Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio, which measures how much energy your air conditioner uses during the annual cooling season. The higher the SEER rating, the less energy your unit uses to cool your home.

You may also see “SEER2,” a newer efficiency standard introduced in 2023 that uses updated testing conditions meant to better reflect real-world performance. SEER2 numbers are typically slightly lower than SEER ratings for the same unit, but they represent the same idea: higher numbers mean more efficient energy usage.

Recent findings suggest that A product with an Energy Star certification has been rigorously tested by the United States Environmental Protection Agency for its energy efficiency. EPA-recognized laboratories test products to Energy Star specifications to ensure manufacturers produce energy-saving products.

Although testing guidelines change per product category, all items must prove they consume less energy than standard models without compromising performance.

Industry observers note that mini-splits are more permanent and expensive than window or portable air conditioners, so they make the most sense when you proposal to cool the same space for several seasons. Most systems also require professional installation, and larger units may need electrical upgrades before you can install them.

It has been revealed that they’re also not invisible. The indoor air handler usually stays mounted high on the wall year-round, which may bother homeowners who prefer the low-profile look of central air vents. Proper sizing and placement matter, too, since an oversized, undersized, or poorly positioned unit can lead to uneven cooling, wasted energy, or poor humidity control.

Sources indicate that ductless air conditioners cool your home without using the network of ducts that central HVAC systems rely on, notes Lincoln. “The way I explain ductless cooling to homeowners is simple: the system conditions the room directly instead of trying to send cooled air through ductwork first,” she explains.

Instead, ductless air conditioners connect a small outdoor condenser to one or more indoor air handlers using refrigerant lines. Because there’s no ductwork involved, these types of units are often more efficient and easier to install in older homes, additions, or finished spaces where running ducts would be difficult. They also allow for “zoned” cooling, meaning you can control the temperature in individual rooms instead of conditioning the entire house at once.

These systems are also more customizable than a whole-house system. “Where mini-splits really shine is zoning,” explains Lincoln. “One outdoor unit can support multiple indoor heads, so different parts of the house can be conditioned based on how those spaces are actually used.”.

Industry observers note that yes. “A mini-split is just a ductless system made up of an outdoor condenser and one or more indoor air handlers,” claims Lincoln. The terms ductless air conditioner and mini-split are generally used interchangeably, as we have in this guide.

It has been revealed that both describe systems that pair an outdoor condenser with one or more indoor air handlers connected by refrigerant lines instead of ductwork. The “split” part refers to the system being divided between indoor and outdoor components.

Some mini-splits provide cooling only, but many modern models are actually heat pumps, meaning they can both cool and heat your home using the same system. Adding air conditioning to an older home that previously utilized radiator or baseboard heat can be tricky—squeezing ductwork into closets and unused corners feels a bit like remodelling Jenga. These units solve that issue without much fuss.

Usually, yes. In most cases, it makes sense to hire a professional. Installing a mini-split usually involves mounting indoor and outdoor units, running refrigerant lines, and making electrical connections, which is why many manufacturers recommend professional installation.

Recent findings suggest that “Installation is where good equipment gets made—or wasted,” advises Lincoln. “Mini-splits look deceptively simple once they’re on the wall, but installation is not casual work. Line sets, electrical, drainage, vacuuming the system down properly before startup…those are the steps that determine whether the unit runs the way it was engineered to run.”.

Recent findings suggest that some systems are more DIY-friendly, but even those can be complicated if you’re not comfortable working with electrical systems or HVAC equipment. Professional installation also helps ensure the system runs efficiently and may be required to maintain the manufacturer’s warranty. If you are a very seasoned DIY pro who’s handy with a YouTube tutorial, you might be okay. Otherwise, we recommend budgeting for an installer.

Companies size mini-splits systems based on BTUs, which measure how much heating or cooling power the unit can deliver.

It has been revealed that “When people ask how to calculate the right BTU for a room, the honest answer is that manufacturer charts are a starting point, not a finish line,” says Lincoln. “For a window unit, those charts can get you close. For a mini-split, a proper load calculation is the better answer.” This is another reason it’s great to work with an expert installer before ordering—they can guide your purchasing based on your needs.

Lincoln explains that it’s not a straightforward calculation, in most cases. “Room size is only the starting point. Sun exposure, ceiling height, insulation, window size, window direction, occupancy, and heat from electronics or appliances all change the cooling load,” she adds.

Smaller systems around 9,000 BTU often work for bedrooms or small offices, while 12,000–18,000-BTU systems handle larger living areas. As a rough rule, most homeowners look at units sized for the square footage of the space they want to heat or cool, but must consider all of these other factors, too.

Breaking: An El Niño amped by climate change has California bracing for the worst

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready.
  • Sources indicate that what is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves.
  • It has been revealed that californians know all too well the threat.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready. The state has strategically stockpiled sandbags, pumps and generators. Debris has been fished out to clear storm drains, seepage blankets shore up aging levees and dams, and wire mesh cages hold back precariously placed boulders.

Sources indicate that what is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves. The fury of this year’s El Niño is being unleashed around the globe as well, from inundating Florida with floods to exacerbating drought in the Amazon. And much more is still to come, forecasts show, with the peak of the climate phenomenon expected to arrive between November 2026 and January 2027.

It has been revealed that californians know all too well the threat. El Niño has historically brought relentless rainfall to the state, flooding cities and triggering landslides.

Industry observers note that state officials learned a lot about preparedness and emergency water management from previous El Niños — particularly the strong event that spanned the winter of 1997–1998. But this year’s event is likely to be even more challenging, a “Super” El Niño superimposed on the backdrop of global climate change.

Climate change has made water management in California more complicated than it was just 30 years ago — as it has elsewhere around the world, states environmental scientist Letitia Grenier, the director of water policy at the Public Policy Institute of California, a nonprofit, nonpartisan think tank based in San Francisco.

In 1997, California’s overall climate was much drier; El Niño brought a big, long rainy season that spanned the state, Grenier says. But now, “it’s just so humid. The air is warmer, so it can hold more water.”.

It has been revealed that that waterlogged atmosphere means that even without El Niño, there’s been less of a distinct rainy season in California, and more rapid flip-flop between intense episodes of rain dumped on the ground followed by periods of heat and dryness. “It’s these strange, erratic patterns that we’ve never seen before,” she indicates. And the state is bracing for how the Super El Niño will clash with this new climate normal.

1997 was the year that the term “El Niño” shot to global fame. It was the most powerful El Niño in recorded history, and the first to be scientifically monitored in real time, continuously tracked by satellites and breathlessly reported on by news outlets. El Niño’s rise to household name status was even cemented in pop culture by an appearance on Saturday Night Live, in a classic sketch by comedian Chris Farley.

It has been revealed that but the event was no laughing matter. It caused global devastation during its brief reign. El Niño events form as westward-blowing trade winds over the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean weaken, allowing warm water to accumulate at the surface. Those waters can then release massive amounts of heat to the atmosphere, altering the position of the Pacific jet stream and helping to disrupt global weather patterns.

Sources indicate that in 1997–1998, global temperatures spiked by 1.5 degrees Celsius on average. Along with the torrential rains in California, the event brought brutal drought to Southeast Asia and deadly summer floods to central Europe and Peru. Record-breaking floods also hit East Africa, which in turn triggered a surge in mosquito-borne Rift Valley fever. The oceans were so warm that 16 percent of the world’s reefs died.

In all, the El Niño–related weather extremes were linked to more than 22,000 fatalities around the world, including nearly 200 in the United States, and an estimated $5.7 trillion in global economic losses.

It has been revealed that not every El Niño is equally intense, or impacts weather in quite the same way. “There’s a lot of variability event to event,” indicates Washington, D.C.–based climate scientist Tom Di Liberto, of the nonprofit climate news organization Climate Central.

In a recent development, but there is a general overall pattern to how El Niño tends to affect weather around the planet, Di Liberto says. For example, there tend to be more tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean, and fewer in the Atlantic — a pattern also observed in 2026.

It has been revealed that el Niño also tends to flatten and accelerate the Pacific jet stream, shifting its flow southward, notes Mike Anderson, California’s state climatologist for the Department of Water Resources, who is based in Sacramento. And that has historically meant that a conveyor belt of back-to-back moisture-loaded storms is set on a collision course with the U.S. West Coast.

Sources indicate that the El Niño rapidly strengthened during the summer of 2026. As westerly trade winds weakened, warm waters accumulated in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, raising both ocean temperatures and the sea level height (shown in this animation). Red and white colors indicate the highest sea level. Beginning in April and intensifying through November, the El Niño event generated Kelvin waves, massive swells that sweep eastward along the equator toward the Americas.

The 1997–1998 El Niño revealed just how devastating that pattern could be in California.

As much as 30 centimeters inundated parts of the state during the month of February 1998 alone. Storm winds and high surf pounded the coast, while rivers swelled and overtopped their banks. Flooding from the “Groundhog Day Storm” destroyed some 1,700 homes in Bay Area cities Palo Alto and Menlo Park. On February 6 near Rio Nido, about 100 kilometers from San Francisco, a forested hillside suddenly crumbled, sending a wall of mud rushing down the mountain. It destroyed about 30 homes.

Landslides also threatened homes and lives in Southern California.

On February 23, then 25-year-old Jenifer Segraves and her fiancé Glenn Flook were living in an apartment on Laguna Canyon Road, in the city of Laguna Beach. The heavy rains had saturated the neighborhood’s steep hillsides, making the terrain unstable.

“We lived up against a hill in the canyon, so there were stairs up to our apartment,” Segraves says now. “They became like a waterfall. I remember my fiancé carrying me up the stairs because there was so much water.” Segraves called her father, Gary Segraves, in a panic, asking for help. Then, the slope behind the building failed, the apartment flooded and she and Flook fled into the rushing mud.

Sources indicate that “We were strong enough to get out, but we were waist-high in mud,” Segraves said. “[My dad] almost drowned getting to us.” All three took shelter at a neighbor’s house, where they showered and hunkered down to wait out the rain.

Around midnight on February 24, the second mudslide arrived.

In a recent development, the neighbor’s “whole house went down,” Segraves says. She escaped through a second-floor window, but her fiancé fell through the floor and was knocked out. He didn’t make it out.

It has been revealed that gary Segraves, meanwhile, was swept down the hillside and landed in a pile of rubble against a rocky cliff. Battered and missing his glasses, he looked around and saw what looked like a doll.

According to recent reports, he reached for the little form — and discovered that it was a baby, very cold but alive. Somehow, the 9-month-old had survived being swept out of her crib from a nearby home. The little girl “wouldn’t have survived if he hadn’t picked her up,” Segraves says.

The havoc wreaked across California by the event 30 years ago cast a stark light on the desperate need to expand waterways, maintain infrastructure and coordinate emergency services, Grenier notes. “An engineering system can only work as well as its capacity.”.

Much of the state’s infrastructure is deteriorating. An October 13 report by the California state auditor noted that the condition of dams and levees across the state “remains a high-risk matter,” with some 57 dams in the state in poor or unsatisfactory condition. “Poorly maintained dams and levees continue to pose a risk to public safety,” the report stated.

California’s water management system was also originally designed specifically to simply shunt excess water away from residential areas, rather than try to capture the water or help it infiltrate into aquifers, Grenier says. But that system worked for a different climate, one that wasn’t so prone to “weather whiplash” — wild, sudden swings between extremely wet and extremely dry conditions.

Alongside punishing, drenching back-to-back storms called atmospheric rivers, the state has also experienced frequent episodes of drought, including two recent severe events, one lasting from 2012 to 2016 and another from 2021 to 2025.

Those years of drought, dwindling snow and pumping too much water from aquifers have dramatically depleted the state’s subsurface water stores. And the heavy rains don’t necessarily help; the torrents of water mostly run off across the surface instead of infiltrating soils to reach the underground aquifer.

According to recent reports, such hydroclimate whiplash isn’t unique to California by any means. It’s a global problem, and it’s becoming more common. A small increase in air temperatures can give a big boost to the atmosphere’s capacity to hold water vapor, increasing that capacity by about 7 percent for every 1 degree C of temperature increase. All of that water vapor has contributed to an increase in extreme precipitation events around the globe since the mid-20th century.

Precipitation is just half of the problem. Rising air temperatures also make the air “thirstier,” causing it to draw even more moisture out of vegetation, soil and surface bodies of water during drier periods — which makes the land more vulnerable to severe drought and wildfire.

In a recent development, it’s now clear that these hydrodynamic shifts have been increasing the frequency of weather whiplash events around the world over the last 75 years or so, scientists reported in 2025. And that whiplash is likely to increase as the world warms more.

Months before reaching peak intensity, the 2026–2027 Super El Niño has begun making its presence known. The Amazon is suffering under intense heat and drought, priming the region for wildfires and pushing the forest closer to a worrisome possible fate: a transition from tropical forest to savanna grasslands. Fires have also begun blazing across Southeast Asia, while heavy rains began inundating the Horn of Africa in October. Arriving on the heels of severe drought, that one-two punch could devastate the region’s crops and pasturelands.

In a recent development, in California, the first harbingers of the arrival of the Super El Niño appeared in early September. Heavy surf pounded the coastline. Regions from San Francisco to Los Angeles saw record high tides by late October that flooded city streets and battered coastlines and seawalls, even as the skies remained clear.

The waves were amped up by an unfortunate trifecta: higher sea levels due to climate change; a lunar cycle that exerted its maximum pull on the tides; and an El Niño–linked phenomenon called Kelvin waves.

Kelvin waves are massive, slow-moving swells of warm ocean water, part of the complicated interplay between wind and water that produces the El Niño Southern Oscillation, the overall weather pattern that includes El Niño and counterpart La Niña events, notes Josh Willis, an oceanographer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif.

As prevailing west-blowing winds weaken over the tropical eastern Pacific, Willis says, water normally pushed west by the winds instead sloshes back eastward. Kelvin waves have historically given a boost to sea levels along the U.S. West Coast of as much as 30 centimeters. This year, that impact could be larger, researchers reported September 30 in a preprint study posted on EarthArXiv.org. Computer model simulations suggest that the risk of the risk of extreme sea levels could be 10 times higher during this El Niño year than during previous events, for coastlines from Alaska all the way to Chile.

Recent findings suggest that then, by late October, the Santa Ana winds arrived: Hot, dry gusts blowing down the mountains toward the coast, fanning wildfires in Southern California. The fires scarred the landscape, denuding it of vegetation, roots that helped stabilize and fortify the soil. Such loosened soil is more likely to become mobilized into a debris flow during heavy rains.

Those rains are now on the way. By mid-November, researchers began tracking storms headed for California. The peak of El Niño is expected to arrive by late November or early December and persist through February or March.

Sources indicate that segraves, after surviving nearly 30 years ago, claims she is aware that another El Niño is coming. But she hasn’t been following the news closely. She’s placed herself on a news diet since her ordeal. She refused to speak to media for years, or even read the coverage about her own story.

It has been revealed that “Everyone wanted to talk to me and I just wanted to be left alone,” she says. Staying away from the news “freed me from all that. It changed my view on life. I take each day as it comes.”.

According to recent reports, but, she adds, one lesson has stayed with her. “I swore I would never live on a cliff again.”.

Trump’s ‘invasion’ asylum ban to face justices

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (559 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The border wall is seen in 2021 stretching along the U.S.-Mexico border near Columbus, N.M.
  • The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.
  • In a recent development, the Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The border wall is seen in 2021 stretching along the U.S.-Mexico border near Columbus, N.M. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.

In a recent development, the Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit that held the president could not broadly deny asylum claims under federal law. The case is the latest high-profile fight over one of Trump’s signature domestic policies.

The administration argues in its petition for the justices to take the case that the president has broad authority over asylum claims, which includes shutting down the system entirely because he has decided he will not grant any.

According to recent reports, “The proclamation thus lawfully suspends access to asylum, which is a purely discretionary benefit. The court of appeals’ insistence that aliens are entitled to file futile asylum applications elevates empty procedures over substance,” the petition states.

According to recent reports, trump issued the order on his first day in office, declaring an “invasion” on the southern border and using that as a reason to deny asylum claims by refugees who present themselves there. The order is still in place, preventing asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border while the lawsuit plays out.

In court filings asking the justices to take the case, the administration pointed to “dramatic” reductions in illegal border crossings, which freed up resources to combat human trafficking and other threats.

In Friday’s order, the justices agreed to hear arguments over the legality of Trump’s executive order as well as whether the lower-court judge could grant an order in favor of all asylum seekers rather than just the ones who brought the suit.

Immigration rights groups initially challenged the order and won a successful ruling from a federal judge in Washington. The administration later appealed to the D.C. Circuit, where it lost at a three-judge panel before it brought the case before the justices.

The D.C. Circuit held that although federal law provides a president discretion in denying asylum claims, he cannot do so categorically.

The ACLU and immigrant rights groups who brought the case defended the ruling in their own filing. The filing argues that Congress mandated the creation of the asylum system and the president “may not invent by fiat a new removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.”.

Last term the justices ruled in favor of a separate policy dating to the first Trump administration that allowed officials to prevent asylum claims by stopping refugees from actually reaching the U.S. border.

A ruling in favor of the refugees could allow the administration to restart that policy and still deny asylum claims.

The case granted Friday is the latest high-profile immigration policy clash on the justices’ docket this term. Earlier this year the justices agreed to hear a challenge to the administration’s policy that most immigrants facing deportation should be detained without bond.

The justices will likely hear oral arguments and decide the case granted Friday before the end of the court’s term next June.

According to recent reports, the case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services.

The libido drug women want is testosterone

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (638 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, these days, Jessica Yih spends a lot of time talking to women about testosterone.
  • It has been revealed that some non-hormonal treatments are now available, but the U.S.
  • Recent findings suggest that not many studies have looked at testosterone’s effects on libido in premenopausal women, but preliminary data in that area are also promising, according to a 2026 research review in The Journal of Sexual Medicine that Yih coauthored.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, these days, Jessica Yih spends a lot of time talking to women about testosterone. Interest is “coming from all directions,” says the University of California, Irvine Health urologist. A major source: women who hope testosterone can boost the female libido. Only about a decade ago, women looking for libido treatments had few medical options — even though women of all ages struggle with low sexual desire.

It has been revealed that some non-hormonal treatments are now available, but the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has yet to approve a female testosterone product, despite years of research suggesting it can boost sexual function and desire among postmenopausal women. Female testosterone products are approved in countries including the United Kingdom and Australia.

Recent findings suggest that not many studies have looked at testosterone’s effects on libido in premenopausal women, but preliminary data in that area are also promising, according to a 2026 research review in The Journal of Sexual Medicine that Yih coauthored. “I have seen it change people’s lives,” Yih indicates. The hormone seems to make the female brain more receptive to sexual stimuli; it also promotes physical effects that enhance sexual pleasure, such as increased blood flow to the genitals. Right now, American women interested in these potential benefits have to look for them off-label. But that may change. In September, the FDA held a public meeting on testosterone use among menopausal women, “with the goal of informing future research and potential drug development in this area,” says Kaveeta Vasisht, the FDA’s associate commissioner for women’s health.

Sources indicate that the hormone has a rocky regulatory past. In 2004, an FDA advisory panel unanimously voted against approving a testosterone patch for women, citing a lack of safety data. There are still outstanding questions on that front, Yih indicates—like how, if at all, long-term use affects risk of conditions such as breast cancer and heart disease. Then, in 2011, a pair of Phase III trials found that testosterone therapy didn’t significantly outperform a placebo — a benchmark the FDA looks for when deciding whether to approve a new drug. That’s not to say testosterone didn’t work, says Tami Rowen, an ob-gyn at UC San Francisco. Rather, it seemed that hype about the hormone was so strong that study participants went in with sky-high expectations, leading even the placebo group to report benefits. The treatment was a “victim of its own success,” Rowen says.

Interest hasn’t let up, though. By one estimate, the U.S. female prescription rate for all uses rose from 0.4 out of every 1,000 women in 2018, to 1.8 out of every 1,000 women in 2026. That’s an increase of nearly 400 percent. With so much buzz, the potential placebo effect remains “the biggest problem with testosterone right now,” Rowen notes.

Another outstanding question, Yih says, is whether using testosterone long-term increases the risk of breast cancer and heart disease.

Women seeking a libido boost do have non-hormonal options. In 2015, the FDA approved Addyi, the first treatment for low libido in premenopausal women. The drug seemingly raises levels of neurotransmitters that promote sexual desire while tamping down those that block it. A competitor, Vyleesi, hit shelves in 2019. Then, last year, regulators expanded Addyi’s use to postmenopausal women younger than 65. An international group of experts, including Rowen, issued recommendations for treating low female libido in 2025 in Sexual Medicine Reviews. Psychological therapies and Addyi are backed by the strongest evidence, the group found.

Sources indicate that rowen currently has her eye on in-development products including Lybrido. The drug, which is slated to enter a Phase III clinical trial in Europe, aims to rev sex drive in the brain and enhance physical arousal. The demand for newly introduced treatments is there, Rowen claims. “Women deserve better than placebo.”.

It has been revealed that countertop ice makers either use water from a built-in reservoir or a connected water line, but the former is most common. You’ll need to refill a reservoir ice maker with water when it runs out. The major benefit is it doesn’t require any plumbing connections—you just fill the tank and it’s ready to use. Yes, it’s perfectly safe to leave most ice makers on during the day and night. Of course, if you’re not using the ice, you will be using electricity to keep it running.

#54279. Industry News: This year’s El Niño is unlike any other on record

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (254 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencenews ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: This year’s El Niño is unlike any other on record

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (254 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was an unprecedented year for El Niño, the weather-changing ocean pattern defined by warmer-than-normal surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific.
  • Sources indicate that in September, the region’s daily average sea surface temperature reached the most extreme level ever recorded: more than 3.03 degrees Celsius above the 30-year average (dashed line).
  • According to recent reports, all that hot water has fueled the most active Pacific hurricane season on record.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was an unprecedented year for El Niño, the weather-changing ocean pattern defined by warmer-than-normal surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. By October 18, the ocean area that researchers use to monitor El Niño’s severity climbed to an average temperature of over 30° Celsius (86° Fahrenheit) for the first time in history. From there, it kept on rising.

Sources indicate that in September, the region’s daily average sea surface temperature reached the most extreme level ever recorded: more than 3.03 degrees Celsius above the 30-year average (dashed line). The World Meteorological Organization predicts that sea surface temperatures may peak at 3.7 degrees above that average by January. The two previous strongest El Niños on record emerged in 1997 and 2015.

According to recent reports, all that hot water has fueled the most active Pacific hurricane season on record. By mid-October, 331 units of cyclone energy had accumulated, beating out 2018’s record of 318 units. It has also unleashed heat into the atmosphere, affecting distant circulation patterns and leading to an extraordinarily quiet Atlantic hurricane season.

2026’s El Niño will be felt well beyond the Upcoming Year. Precipitation and drought impacts are expected across the world through spring 2027. And the global heating effect could compound with human-caused climate warming to make 2027 the hottest year ever recorded.

Sources indicate that the heat that El Niño unleashes into the atmosphere shifts storm tracks and weather patterns globally. Here are some of the most significant observed and anticipated effects.

Mussels that live in total darkness have cells that still keep a daily rhythm

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1144 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Deep-sea mussels live in total darkness, yet their cells kept a roughly 24-hour rhythm in the lab, offering clues to how life keeps time without sunlight.
  • Deep in the Atlantic, a mussel called Bathymodiolus azoricus lives where no daylight reaches, and the tides, not the sun, change its surroundings on a schedule.
  • Even so, the mussel’s cells kept a daily rhythm when researchers grew them in a lab refrigerator, far from the seafloor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Deep-sea mussels live in total darkness, yet their cells kept a roughly 24-hour rhythm in the lab, offering clues to how life keeps time without sunlight.

Deep in the Atlantic, a mussel called Bathymodiolus azoricus lives where no daylight reaches, and the tides, not the sun, change its surroundings on a schedule.

Even so, the mussel’s cells kept a daily rhythm when researchers grew them in a lab refrigerator, far from the seafloor.

The finding suggests that genes that run daily clocks in flies and people also help keep time in animals that never see sunlight.

Audrey Mat, a researcher at the Alfred Wegener Institute in Germany and the University of Vienna, grew the cells from mussels collected on the Atlantic seafloor.

Her team has kept two of those cultures alive for more than three and a half years.

The mussels come from the Lucky Strike vent field on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, south of the Azores, about 5,600 feet (1,700 meters) down. The water pressure there is about 170 times what it is at sea level.

At hydrothermal vents, seawater seeps into the seafloor, moves through the rock below and flows back out as hot, metal-rich fluid. Some of it reaches about 660°F (350°C).

Recent findings suggest that the mussels settle in cooler water nearby, between 39 and 48°F (4 and 9°C). The direction of the vent flow shifts with the tides, so the water around the mussels switches between vent fluid and ordinary seawater.

In a 2020 study, Mat and her colleagues reported that on the seafloor, the mussels’ behavior and gene activity followed mainly a tidal rhythm of about 12.4 hours.

A weaker daily rhythm indicated up as well, though no clear day-night cycle reaches the vents.

Mussels from a shallower vent switched to a mostly daily pattern in a lab with lights on for 12 hours and off for 12 hours.

How an animal with no brain produces either rhythm has been unclear.

Industry observers note that lab cells are usually kept warm, close to body temperature. Mat tried something different.

“While cells in the laboratory usually thrive at 25 to 37 °C, our mussel cells grow in the fridge, at deep-sea temperatures,” stated Mat, who first proposed the experiments.

“This technical advance is unique in the world and allows novel insights into the biology of these animals.”.

In a recent development, the team tried cells from six tissues at three temperatures. At 77°F (25°C), fungi and other contaminants swiftly took over.

It has been revealed that out of 63 cultures, cells from the mussel’s foot survived best. The foot is the muscular part a mussel extends from its shell.

Keeping whole mussels alive took work too.

About half of the animals collected in 2023 died within a month, likely from the stress of the trip to the surface and the flight to Vienna.

The remaining mussels lived for 13 months in an aquarium shielded from white light.

It has been revealed that to look for a clock, the team put foot tissue from five mussels in culture and kept it in constant darkness at 39°F (4°C). Then they sampled the cells every four hours for two days.

A pattern of gene activity that repeats about every 24 hours is called a circadian rhythm. Finding one is how scientists spot a clock at work.

In a recent development, of 5,616 genes the team could track, 157 highlighted a circadian pattern, about 2.8%. That’s close to the 2.5% the team found earlier in mussels on the seafloor.

So the cells kept time on their own, with no ocean and no daylight around them.

Across 10,000 reshuffles of the sampling times, none yielded at least 157 daily cycles while also recovering the same 66 transcripts that earlier research had identified as rhythmic.

The team also found 109 genes with a tidal pattern. That number was no higher than chance alone would produce.

In fruit flies and mammals, CLOCK teams up with a partner protein to turn on clock genes such as period.

The proteins those genes produce then dial back CLOCK and its partner, and the cycle starts again.

No genome exists yet for this mussel. So the team compared three related deep-sea mussels and found two stretches of DNA, just upstream of period, that were nearly identical across species.

The researchers copied those stretches from B. azoricus and tested them in fruit fly cells that lack their own clock parts.

The mussel’s CLOCK and BMAL proteins increased the activity of a test gene controlled by one of those DNA segments.

According to recent reports, A protein called CRY2 shut the signal down, and more CRY2 meant a stronger effect. The mussel’s PER protein had no effect on its own.

Added alongside CRY2, though, PER made the shut-off stronger and helped CRY2 build up inside the cell’s nucleus. A third protein, TIM, canceled PER’s effect.

The PER result matters because the period gene in these mussels rises and falls on a roughly tidal schedule.

The researchers suggest the balance between PER and CRY2 could switch the clock between tidal and daily timing.

The deep sea is one of the least explored ecosystems on Earth, and plans for deep-sea mining are putting it under pressure.

Kristin Tessmar-Raible, who studies biological clocks at the University of Oldenburg and the University of Vienna, led the study with Marjolaine Matabos of Ifremer, France’s national ocean research institute.

“The fact that these ecosystems are mechanistically highly complex and possess timing systems as sophisticated as those at the surface underlines how worthy of protection they are,” Tessmar-Raible and Matabos remarked.

Industry observers note that “On land, we know that human activities such as light or vibrations disrupt circadian clocks. Deep-sea clocks are very likely just as vulnerable, with significant consequences for organisms and ecosystems.”.

The team noted that mining could affect the timing of deep-sea animals even from a great distance.

A dish of cells doesn’t capture everything happening inside a whole mussel at a vent.

The team also detected RNA from the period gene in mussel tissue, while levels in the cultured cells were below what the test could detect.

Either the cells with a tidal rhythm didn’t survive in culture, or conditions in the dish turned off whatever drives the tidal pattern of period, the researchers wrote.

Sources indicate that the next question is whether a mussel runs one clock that switches between tides and days, or keeps separate groups of cells that each follow one rhythm. The researchers wrote that their results fit either idea.

Genome studies and work locating the clock proteins inside mussel tissue could help tell those two ideas apart, the team wrote.

The full study was published in the journal EMBO Reports.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that winter will be here before you know it. Easily one of the most laborious and hated chores of that season is shoveling the snow. Not only that, it can be dangerous. Beyond the strain it puts on your back, the American Heart Association states it can increase the risk of a cardiac event for those with heart issues, and the cold weather can hide symptoms that otherwise would give you pause. That’s why the best electric snow shovels not only make the task easier, but safer, too, for those at risk.

Recent findings suggest that of course, you should not mistake these for full-blown snowblowers. Because of their compact size and throwing range, electric snow shovels are best used for small homes with shorter walkways and fewer steps. Like their larger counterparts, they use augers to scoop up snow (no more than 6 to 8 inches, ideally) and launch it up to 25 feet through the air so you don’t have to bend or lift as you dig out after a storm.

They also work well as supplemental tools for clearing out outdoor stairs, walkways, patios, decks, and anywhere else a snowblower may not be able to reach. If that sounds like it could help you out of a blizzard-induced jam this winter, we can steer you toward the best electric snow shovels that can make the chore as painless as possible.

Toro Power Shovel 60-Volt 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel.

As a top name in yard tools, we are interested to see what Toro’s take on simple snow removal is.

Ego Power+ EGO POWER+ 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel.

In a recent development, ego has several models of electric now shovels. This one has adjustable fins to let you guide the direction of the snow you remove.

We leaned on our personal experience with snow removal machines and conducted extensive research to inform our selections. Specifically, we looked at each machine’s clearing area, weight, battery life, and throwing distance. Because snow removal needs vary from property to property, we included larger models that can clear up to 6 inches of snow from two- to four-car driveways, along with lighter electric snow shovels that are easy to lift and maneuver in smaller areas, such as walkways and patios.

Though we still include one corded model as our best budget pick, we primarily focus on cordless models because for most people these days, the convenience of battery power beats having to drag a cord around on a cold day.

Most electric snow shovels max out with a fairly narrow clearing width and low clearing depth, potentially forcing you to do multiple passes to clear a proper path. This Earthwise model is an exception.

Industry observers note that with a broad clearing width of 16 inches and a depth of 8 inches, it’s capable of clearing paths through deeper snow. And since it debuts snow up to 32 feet away, you can use this machine to clear small driveways along with your walkways, deck, and patio.

On the other hand, this electric snow shovel is quite heavy. It has wheels, though, which make it easier to push and maneuver. It’s a tradeoff, but one that pays off if you live in an area that routinely gets 6 to 8 inches of snow in a night.

According to recent reports, you may notice that our best overall is a bit cheaper than our best value pick. This is because we felt the wide clearing width and the fact that it has wheels to support your efforts made this a solid choice for many people.

Though higher in price than some of the other models on our list, there’s a lot that you get for the price, namely power and run time. With a larger battery than most, this electric shovel from Greenworks runs longer on a single battery than any other cordless electric snow shovel out there.

In a recent development, it packs a good amount of power with a large 80-volt 4.0-amp-hour battery powering a brushless motor; you’ll get about 45 minutes of run time on a single charge. This snow shovel clears a 12-inch path through up to 6 inches of snow, then blows it 25 feet away, making it ideal for uncovering a large area after a light snowfall.

It has been revealed that just remember that with great power and runtime comes great weight. With the battery loaded, this machine weighs more than 19 pounds, so moving it around for 45 minutes can turn into a real workout.

Sources indicate that if you want the most clearing power possible from an electric snow shovel, Earthwise is your brand. This corded model can carve a 16-inch-wide path through snow up to 8 inches high, which is significantly more than what you can expect from other brands. It’s also significantly more powerful, moving up to 430 pounds of snow per minute.

For reference, most of our other picks move around 300 pounds per minute. As a result, it can handle deeper, slushier snow than most electric snow shovels. It also has a longer throwing distance than most corded or cordless electric snow shovels out there.

At 16 pounds, it’s pretty heavy, but like other heavy models, it has a pair of wheels so you can push it most of the time. In short, it offers the best snow removal capability of any machine this side of a snowblower.

Ryobi makes several types of cordless electric snow shovels, but this model is a head attachment for its Expand-It 40-Volt String Trimmer that you can swap in when the snow starts falling. The advantage here is that you aren’t limited to just one tool; you can swap in a variety of attachments to run on the same primary unit and battery. This makes a lot of sense if it only snows a couple of times where you live, and you only need a snow thrower infrequently.

Recent findings suggest that during our testing, we were impressed with this tool’s performance. In mere minutes, we were able to clear a wide path through 8 inches of snow (more than the max height of 6 inches this model is rated for) on a patio outside our office. It was not fresh snow, either; it was densely packed after sitting for several days. There were times when the shovel head froze up while trying to push through too much at once, but this was rapidly rectified by pulling back and pushing through again. The snow flies quite far, too, for such a small toolhead, at least 10 to 15 feet by our estimation.

Being able to fling snow that far is a good thing because this thrower can only send the snow straight forward (some models have adjustable fins that allow you to send it to either side). You need to be strategic about the direction you push to avoid creating more work for yourself if you have a long path to clear.

According to recent reports, we must admit, too, that while this electric snow shovel makes the job easier than a manual shovel, it does take a bit of strength to operate, especially since it doesn’t have wheels to help you stay balanced and moving. You can move it along the ground, but you may need to lift it slightly if the snow is packed or icy at the lower levels, and it doesn’t come with a shoulder strap to help you do that. If you aim to greatly reduce the physical strain of snow removal, models from our list that feature wheels and directional fins may be a better option.

Sources indicate that overall, if you already have the Ryobi 40-volt-compatible string trimmer, adding this attachment to your arsenal would be a good move if you only need to clear snow from a small driveway, walkway, deck, or patio. The 40-volt, 4-amp-hour battery will give you up to an hour of power, which is more than enough for a small job like that, and buying into this multitool system will keep it from being a tool that just sits in the toolshed or basement for most of the time.

Recent findings suggest that the lightweight design of this cordless electric snow shovel makes it a great option if other electric snow shovels are too heavy for you to manage. Whereas most electric snow shovels weigh around 18 pounds, this one weighs just 13.5 pounds.

Sources indicate that along with being lighter, the Snow Joe electric snow shovel also has a dual-handle design that allows you to operate it while standing up straight, taking pressure off your back. Despite its lighter weight, it can still clear a foot-wide path of snow up to 6 inches deep. The Snow Joe does have a shorter runtime than most, which limits it to lighter-duty snow removal, such as clearing walks, decks, and patios.

Industry observers note that with its two 20-volt rechargeable batteries, the Worx electric snow shovel is both versatile and powerful. It can clear a path a foot wide and up to 6 inches deep and throw snow up to 25 feet, so it's suitable for clearing tighter spaces.

The two-battery design gives you the option to mix and match larger-capacity 20-volt Worx batteries to increase this shovel’s run time for larger jobs, such as clearing small driveways. It also comes with a dual charger, so you can charge both batteries simultaneously for a shorter turnaround time.

Another plus is that this model's batteries are compatible with other 20-volt Worx yard machines, making it a great option if you’ve already bought into the Worx product line.

It has been revealed that we’d be remiss if we didn’t point out that this whole category of yard machines has some limitations. Most electric snow shovels can only handle snow depths up to 6 inches—8 inches if you’re lucky—and lack the power to handle heavier slushy snow. They are ideally suited to powdery snow on walkways, patios, decks, and maybe a small driveway. If you see heavy snowfalls regularly or have a large number of driveways and parking spaces to clear, get a snowblower before you buy an electric snow shovel. For substantial jobs, go with a gas snowblower. An electric snowblower works for small to moderate-sized driveways.

It has been revealed that when push comes to shove, we recommend looking for a cordless electric snow shovel rather than a corded one. Having the freedom to move without worrying about a cord makes the whole shoveling or snowblowing process much easier. That said, if you’re on a tight budget or only need to clear a short walk or a small patio or deck that’s near an outdoor outlet, you can get by with a corded model.

Much like a snowblower, electric snow shovels are rated by how much snow they can move. The wider the shovel, the fewer passes it takes to clear an area. Most electric snow shovels move a 10- to 16-inch-wide path of snow. A small, narrow shovel is lighter and more nimble, making it useful for creating pathways. Wider, larger models are better equipped for clearing a patio or driveway, but are also heavier and more difficult to maneuver in tighter spaces.

Electric snow shovels can handle snowbanks around 4 to 8 inches high, depending on their clearing depth. Technically, you can remove deeper snowfall with these machines, but you’ll have to make more passes to do so.

It has been revealed that for an electric snow shovel to be useful, it should be able to propel the snow far enough that it’s off the deck, walkway, or driveway that you’re clearing. Most electric snow shovels launch their snow between 20 and 30 feet, which is on par with entry-level, corded electric snowblowers, but shorter than cordless and gas snowblowers that can throw snow a distance of 40 feet or more. With that in mind, consider the route you plan to take while clearing, and make sure you’re moving the snow somewhere out of the way so it can sit until spring arrives.

Electric snow shovels process and throw snow like a snowblower, so you won’t need to bend over and scoop up snow as you would with a shovel. However, you should still look for the lightest possible option. While you won’t have to lift and throw snow as you would with a conventional snow shovel, you have to hold it upright and apply some force to push it through the snow. At the very least, you should look for a shovel that you can lift easily whenever you need to clear steps or multiple levels of patio.

According to recent reports, electric snow shovels typically weigh between 10 and 20 pounds. As you might expect, more powerful shovels that can move more snow and feature large batteries tend to be heavier than smaller, narrower models. Some large electric snow shovels have a set of wheels mounted to the rear of the base for standing upright on their own, so you can maneuver the machine with minimal lifting.

Similar to standard snow shovels, electric models come in both straight and curved handle varieties. A curved handle allows for standing more upright while operating the machine, putting less strain on your lower back and decreasing the risk of injury. A straight handle gives you more leverage for lifting loads of snow, but since an electric snow shovel has an auger that lifts and blows the snow for you, it’s not an advantage for electric models.

In a recent development, electric snow shovels operate similarly to single-stage snow blowers. The shovel end of the machine has an auger that’s powered by an electric motor. As you push the shovel through the snow, the rotating auger collects snow, mashes it up, and then propels it through a shoot that throws the snow off to the side.

Recent findings suggest that the average electric snow shovel can churn through about 300 pounds of snow per minute. That means a snow shovel with a 12-inch wide intake and a clearing depth of 6 inches can remove about 4 inches of powdery snow from a 1,000 square foot driveway in about 20 minutes.

Just keep in mind that a shovel’s snow-clearing ability varies depending on certain conditions, such as the heft of the snow itself.

In a recent development, it’s never a bad idea to have a standard snow shovel around. While the electric snow shovel can reach most spaces that a standard push-behind snowblower can’t, it may not always be able to clear hardened snow or wet slush.

Plus, a manual shovel ensures that you can always dig out in an emergency, like when you’ve lost power after a snowstorm.

Latest Update: A tiny skull changed the story of human origins, and it’s doing it again

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (821 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Taung Child is about 3 million years old, and a upcoming study suggests some fossils long grouped with it may belong to a different species.
  • A skull the size of an orange changed everything we thought we knew about human origins in 1924.
  • New research has pinned the Taung Child – the original specimen of Australopithecus africanus and the first fossil proof that humans evolved in Africa – to between 2.96 and 3.03 million years old.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Taung Child is about 3 million years old, and a upcoming study suggests some fossils long grouped with it may belong to a different species.

A skull the size of an orange changed everything we thought we knew about human origins in 1924. Now, a century later, it’s doing it again.

New research has pinned the Taung Child – the original specimen of Australopithecus africanus and the first fossil proof that humans evolved in Africa – to between 2.96 and 3.03 million years old.

A more unsettling finding was that many of the fossils long grouped alongside it probably don’t belong there at all.

The study was conducted by an international team led by Gabriele Macho from the Vrije Universiteit Brussel.

The experts combined uranium-lead dating, 3D dental morphometrics, brain development modeling, and fossilized pollen to argue that southern Africa’s early hominin landscape was far messier than textbooks suggest.

Industry observers note that here’s an uncomfortable fact that paleoanthropology has been skirting for decades. Australopithecus africanus – one of the most cited species in human evolution – has never been properly defined.

According to recent reports, the Taung Child is its holotype, the original reference specimen. But no definitive diagnostic criteria were ever established for classifying other fossils into the same species.

Since the 1950s, researchers have lumped dozens of South African fossils under the A. africanus label. However, they used vague qualitative descriptors like “more rounded” and “less extreme.”.

Strictly speaking, the Taung Child remains the only unequivocal member of its own species.

“For over 100 years, we assumed the Taung Child was just one of many similar fossils from the era,” Macho stated.

Industry observers note that “Our findings turn that on its head. The human family tree wasn’t a neat, straight trunk – it was a chaotic, tangled bush driven by climate shifts.”.

The team used 3D geometric morphometrics of the dentino-enamel junction – the boundary between enamel and dentine inside first molars – to compare Taung against other supposed A. africanus specimens.

This internal tooth structure forms early in development. Unlike bone, which remodels through life, it is under strong genetic control.

Sources indicate that taung’s molars fell at the edge of the A. africanus cluster in shape space, equidistant between Sts 18 (a presumed A. africanus) and SK 61 (a Paranthropus robustus).

Other fossils traditionally lumped with Taung – MLD 2 from Makapansgat, Sts 24 from Sterkfontein – looked nothing like it.

Sources indicate that the adult fossils assigned to Australopithecus africanus had braincase volumes ranging from 391 to 568 milliliters. That range is comparable to the variation seen within a single living ape species.

In a recent development, braincase shape raised a different question. Using growth patterns in living apes as a guide, the researchers estimated how the Taung Child’s braincase might have changed by adulthood.

Taung could have developed a braincase shaped like those of two adult fossils, Sts 5 and Sts 60.

In a recent development, three others were harder to explain using the same growth patterns, suggesting that some fossils assigned to A. africanus may belong to a different species.

The team extracted fossilized pollen from cave infills at the Taung site. They found wetland sedges, grasses, and savanna indicators – but also Podocarpus, which is startling.

Today, Podocarpus forests are confined to the wet eastern Escarpment, roughly 400 kilometers northeast of Taung.

Their presence suggests ancient Taung was more wooded than the current dry grassland.

The area was likely a mix of riparian woodland and Bushveld-like savanna stretching across what is today semi-arid Thornveld.

The paper’s most ambitious move is linking all of this to climate.

Hydroclimate records from marine and terrestrial cores show that between 4 and 2.5 million years ago, southern Africa experienced pronounced wet-dry oscillations driven by orbital eccentricity cycles.

The region sits at a critical biogeographic junction, where the tropics bordering the temperate world meet.

That boundary shifted over millions of years as the Intertropical Convergence Zone migrated northward.

The authors propose that early human relatives followed shifting habitats.

As those habitats expanded and contracted, populations may have repeatedly split apart and reconnected, helping explain the diversity seen in the fossils.

A century after its discovery, the Taung Child is still the only specimen that can truly be called Australopithecus africanus. Everything else might be something different.

The authors are blunt. Scientists should stop invoking “intraspecific variation” as a catch-all explanation.

Industry observers note that instead, they should re-examine the historical biases baked into how these fossils were sorted. They should also treat the eco-evolutionary dynamics of Plio-Pleistocene southern Africa as the primary engine of the diversity we see.

The Taung Child isn’t just a museum piece. It’s a provocation and a clear warning against tidy narratives.

The study is published in the journal npj Palaeoecosystems.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists discovered Gonatopus quebecensis, a tiny wasp in Québec that attacks leafhoppers and might help protect crops naturally.
  • Some leafhoppers in Québec farm fields have a small sac stuck to their bodies.
  • Each sac holds a wasp larva that feeds on the leafhopper as it grows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists discovered Gonatopus quebecensis, a tiny wasp in Québec that attacks leafhoppers and might help protect crops naturally.

Some leafhoppers in Québec farm fields have a small sac stuck to their bodies. These insects are known to spread disease to carrots and canola.

Each sac holds a wasp larva that feeds on the leafhopper as it grows.

The wasps were raised to adulthood by researchers, who found a species nobody had named. It has now been called Gonatopus quebecensis.

It belongs to a group known as pincer wasps and is about as long as a sesame seed.

Industry observers note that the wasp is a natural enemy of a crop pest and was already living in the fields. The researchers do not yet know whether it kills enough leafhoppers to help a farmer.

Leafhoppers on the province’s farms have been studied by scientists at Université Laval in Québec City since 2021.

Study supervisor Edel Pérez-López said the sightings “sparked our curiosity about the natural enemies of these crucial agricultural insects.”.

The study itself is a description. Lead author Thomas Vinatier and five colleagues described the wasp’s body and read a stretch of its DNA. The insect it grows on was also identified. The wasp was not tested as pest control.

It has been revealed that in July 2025 the team collected leafhoppers carrying wasp larvae. The insects came from highbush blueberry fields in the Mauricie region of Québec.

They were moved into a university greenhouse where the wasps bred on leafhoppers kept on potted barley. The room was held at 73°F (23°C) and the lights stayed on 18 hours a day.

Recent findings suggest that adult wasps emerged and the colony kept going. One female now serves as the reference specimen for the species. She was reared there in January 2026.

For close study the researchers randomly picked 11 adults. Six were females and five were males. Seven more were dissected so the mouthparts could be examined under a microscope.

The reference female and one male are now stored in Ottawa. They are kept in the Canadian National Collection of Insects, Arachnids and Nematodes. The other specimens stayed at the university.

The fresh species is named after Québec. A total of 55 Gonatopus species are now known from the Nearctic region. That region covers most of North America.

The female has no wings. She is mostly black with brownish-yellow on parts of her legs and antennae. At 0.12 inches (2.97 millimeters) long she could pass for a small ant.

It has been revealed that each of her front legs ends in a pincer. It is made of an enlarged claw and the last segment of the foot. A row of tiny plates is carried on that segment.

Pincers like hers give the family its common name. Females grab their prey with them. The family has 1,928 known species that attack leafhoppers and their relatives.

The male is a little smaller at just under a tenth of an inch (2.41 millimeters). He is almost entirely black and has clear wings.

In a recent development, males and females are hard to match in these parasitic wasps. The two sexes of one species can look very unlike each other. Matching them by eye is therefore unreliable.

In a recent development, rearing helped because both sexes came out of the same colony on the same host. The match was supported by the DNA data.

A short stretch of a gene was read from four wasps. Two were females and two were males. Biologists use that stretch as a DNA barcode because it differs from one species to the next.

No named species in the public databases matched the four wasps. Two unnamed records did.

One was a larva from Québec that the same lab had raised earlier from the same leafhopper species. It was a 99.91% match.

According to recent reports, the other was an unidentified larva from Ontario. It was filed in a reference library of 1.5 million barcodes from Canadian invertebrates.

The Ontario larva’s barcode matched the females’ exactly and the males’ at 99.80%.

Recent findings suggest that the wasp had therefore been collected and sequenced before in two provinces. It may have gone unnamed because no adult specimens were available.

Among the named species compared, Gonatopus pedestris had the most similar DNA barcode, at 95.74%.

Recent findings suggest that only one G. pedestris barcode was available for the comparison. It came from a specimen collected in Norway. The authors wrote that more samples are needed to show how the two species are related.

Industry observers note that the wasp’s host is the aster leafhopper. This insect is about an eighth of an inch (3 to 4 millimeters) long.

The wasp’s larvae develop on the aster leafhopper and feed on it.

An infected aster leafhopper can pass along phytoplasmas as it feeds on a plant. Phytoplasmas are bacteria-like organisms that have no cell wall.

One result is aster yellows, a disease capable of heavy losses in canola and carrots.

The aster leafhopper is abundant on Canadian farms. In Québec strawberry fields it was found more often than any other leafhopper in the team’s earlier surveys.

Spraying has not been a sure answer for these crop pests. Strawberry fields in eastern Canada were examined in a 2024 study by members of the same lab.

They reported that growers’ sprays may not have been keeping leafhopper numbers down.

Industry observers note that the search for the leafhopper’s natural enemies had a second motive. Pérez-López said it was the province’s push to use less insecticide.

The farming question was left open by the researchers. They do not yet know what share of leafhoppers the wasp attacks or at what time of year. It is also unclear whether other leafhopper species are used.

In a recent development, wingless females are poorly sampled by the traps entomologists set for flying insects. Wasps like this one may therefore be undercounted across North America, the authors wrote.

Sources indicate that the team suggested repeating its own method in more places. Leafhoppers that carry wasp larvae would be collected and kept alive until the wasps emerge. The adults can then be matched by body and by DNA.

The authors wrote that such studies must come first. Only then can the wasp’s contribution to pest control be judged.

Sources indicate that three jobs are planned by Pérez-López’s lab. They are a full genome for the wasp, a closer look at its breeding and trials with other leafhopper species.

The full study was published in the journal ZooKeys.
