Hear stars being born in Chandra’s upcoming sonifications

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (929 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every image of the cosmos is a translation of data.
  • Sonification does the same for the ears, turning an object’s brightness, color, and position into pitch, volume, and tone.
  • It has been revealed that our ears are acutely sensitive to shifts in pitch, and researchers in fields ranging from astronomy to volcanology have found that listening to data can reveal patterns a visual plot might hide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every image of the cosmos is a translation of data. The X-rays collected by NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory and the infrared light gathered by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) are invisible to our eyes, so astronomers assign them colors we can see. Even optical observations, from Hubble to backyard astrophotographers, translate, too, often assigning or enhancing color based on emission in various filters.

Sonification does the same for the ears, turning an object’s brightness, color, and position into pitch, volume, and tone. The idea dates back at least to the Geiger counter, invented in 1908, whose clicks intensify as radiation climbs. In 2020, the Chandra X-ray Center released A Universe of Sound, NASA’s first ongoing program to sonify astronomical data.

It has been revealed that our ears are acutely sensitive to shifts in pitch, and researchers in fields ranging from astronomy to volcanology have found that listening to data can reveal patterns a visual plot might hide. Sonification also opens the cosmos to people who are blind or have low vision, for whom a processed image offers little.

RELATED: Listen to the universe: How sonification turns data into sound.

On November 17, Chandra released four new sonifications, each built on a region where stars are forming right now. Young, massive stars blast out X-rays in fierce winds and outbursts, and studying those nurseries helps astronomers reconstruct how stars — the Sun included — got their start. Each piece pairs Chandra’s X-ray data with views from other NASA telescopes.

Sources indicate that each sonification plays as a short video. A line sweeps across the image, and whatever it crosses becomes sound. Most of the regions also come in three versions — Chandra’s X-rays alone, the companion telescope’s data alone, and the full composite. Try a single layer first, then the composite, and you’ll start to hear which sounds are associated with which kind of light.

Recent findings suggest that at around 400 light-years away, the Rho Ophiuchi cloud complex is the closest star-forming region of the four. This crowded region is filled with a wide variety of stars. Chandra’s X-ray data identifies individual newborn stars, while JWST maps the other stars, gas, and dust around them. The X-rays ring out as bright, shimmering notes. Meanwhile, the clouds of dust and gas provide shifting ethereal chords, and individual stars land as crisp, percussive pings. Listen for the hush partway through — that’s a stretch of dark dust that hides almost all light.

About 1,310 light-years away and just below Orion’s Belt, the Orion Nebula is often visible to the naked eye and demonstrates up in even the smallest telescope on a dark night. Chandra reveals more than 1,000 young stars here, each one sparkling in the sonification. Around them, the nebula’s diffuse X-ray glow holds steady as a ringing whistle. JWST’s infrared view of the dust and gas is audible as bent, warbling strings and a synthesized harp, reaching a crescendo in the nebula’s densest region before fading out.

Roughly 7,670 light-years away lies the ridge of gas and dust that became one of JWST’s most famous images when it was released in 2022. Chandra sees the scene differently, cutting through the dust to the hidden infant stars within it. Each of those stars plays as a quick stab, while the region’s faint X-ray glow draws out droning, unhurried notes — all played on an actual cello by musician Johnny Mok. JWST’s towering cliffs are a steady drone underneath, with upcoming instruments chiming in briefly to denote a star or one of the cliffline’s jagged peaks.

Sources indicate that some 12 million light-years away in Ursa Major, M82 is the only object in the album beyond our galaxy. This starburst galaxy is building stars many times faster than the Milky Way. Its newborn giants burn out and explode quickly, venting superheated gas plumes that shine brightly in Chandra’s X-rays. Here, Chandra’s data joins Hubble’s visible-light view and infrared from JWST and the retired Spitzer Space Telescope. X-rays sit at the very top of the register, with the region’s busy center whooshing like moving air, filling most of the audible spectrum. It is punctuated by sharp, short stings from brighter newborn stars. The infrared rumbles below as a low hum interrupted by picked notes, and visible light fills the middle with a variety of sounds, including sweeping chords that rise and fall with optical brightness.

It has been revealed that the Chandra sonifications come from a team led by visualization scientist Kimberly Arcand of the Chandra X-ray Center, working with astrophysicist Matt Russo and musician Andrew Santaguida of the SYSTEM Sounds project and consultant Christine Malec, a blind astronomer and musician. You can hear all four at the Chandra release page, and find the program’s full back catalog at chandra.si.edu/sound.

Where Chandra’s new album is composed by others, Skysynth lets you become the composer. Built by the same SYSTEM Sounds duo of Russo and Santaguida for the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s SkyViewer app, it lets you roam Rubin’s ultra-wide view of the southern sky — press Play to coast, or steer with your arrow keys or by dragging with the mouse. Galaxies crossing the center of the screen strum a harp and stars ring a glockenspiel, with color setting the pitch and brightness the volume.

Try it at skyviewer.app/skysynth.

Brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer at Astronomy, based in Chattanooga, Tennessee, fueled by an unending curiosity about the universe. A former classroom teacher, he has a knack for breaking down complex concepts for a wide audience.

#54272. Brain scans reveal where fractions fit on the mental number line

Brain scans reveal where fractions fit on the mental number line

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1089 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Brain scans show that adults use a shared mental number line to compare fractions and whole numbers, even as the brain distinguishes between them.
  • A quarter looks more like four on the page, but its value is much closer to zero.
  • As adults compared fractions and whole numbers, brain activity followed a shared number line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brain scans show that adults use a shared mental number line to compare fractions and whole numbers, even as the brain distinguishes between them.

A quarter looks more like four on the page, but its value is much closer to zero. In a latest brain scan study, that difference mattered.

As adults compared fractions and whole numbers, brain activity followed a shared number line.

The patterns still distinguished fractions from whole numbers, but numbers close in value tended to produce more similar patterns.

One idea about how the brain handles abstract concepts is that it files related concepts close together, so that similar ideas produce similar patterns of activity.

Numbers are a good way to test that, because everyone agrees on their order.

Daniela Valério and Stanislas Dehaene of the Inserm-CEA Cognitive Neuroimaging Unit, known as Unicog, led the study at the NeuroSpin center outside Paris.

In a recent development, people have long been known to carry a number line in their heads for whole numbers. The team wanted to know whether fractions, which children learn after years of schooling, get added to the same line.

Twenty-two adults took part, all right-handed native French speakers between 19 and 39 who had finished high school with a science track.

Two were excluded, one for a cyst found on the scan and one who had a panic attack in the scanner.

It has been revealed that that left 20 participants in the brain scan analysis. A faulty response button reduced the number to 19 for the analysis of speed and accuracy.

Each person lay in a high-field MRI scanner run by the French research agency CEA. The numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 and the fractions 1/4, 1/3, 1/2, 2/3, 3/2, and 5/2 flashed up one at a time, each for one second.

For every number, the person pressed a button to say whether it was bigger or smaller than the one before.

According to recent reports, each run lasted just under ten minutes, and every number followed every other number exactly once. The fractions were built from the same digits as the whole numbers on purpose.

That let the team tell whether the brain was reading 1/4 as a quarter or as a 1 next to a 4.

Fractions slowed people down. A comparison between two fractions took about 1.2 seconds on average, against 0.8 seconds between two whole numbers.

People also got 9.5 percent of fraction pairs wrong, compared with 3.7 percent of whole number pairs.

In an interview with Earth.com, Valério stated fractions are harder for a few reasons.

Whole numbers follow a simple counting sequence, so 3 is followed by 4, while there is always another fraction between any two different numbers.

In a recent development, the size of a fraction is also not always easy to judge from the numbers in it. “For example, although 5 is greater than 3, 1/5 is smaller than 1/3,” Valério said.

Numbers that were close together were also harder than numbers far apart, whichever kind they were. The closer two numbers were, the slower and less accurate people got, and the effect was strongest when both were fractions.

Psychologists have known this distance effect for whole numbers for decades, and here it held for fractions too.

Sources indicate that the team then laid out the speed and error data as a map. The 12 numbers fell along a single curved line in order of size, with the fractions among the whole numbers where their values belonged.

According to recent reports, the scans demonstrated the same thing. Across the brain regions that handle math, the pattern of activity for each number varied along two main directions.

It has been revealed that one separated fractions from whole numbers. The other ordered all 12 numbers by size, from small to large, and ignored whether they were fractions.

The size ordering was strongest in the intraparietal sulcus, a fold near the top and back of the brain that has long been tied to math.

In a recent development, researchers have also linked this region to the ability to estimate quantities. In the new study, patterns of activity in the hippocampus also reflected how close numbers were in value.

Then the team looked at single points on the cortex.

Within the front part of that parietal fold, many spots responded most to one particular number and less to its neighbors. The spots formed a map, with small numbers at the front and larger numbers farther back.

It has been revealed that the map for fractions matched the map for whole numbers. Spots that preferred 0 also responded to 1/4, 1/3, and 1/2, and 1/4 ended up far from 4.

Valério stated that when people compare numbers, they have to focus on magnitude, meaning how large or small each one is.

“Our study shows that the brain organizes this information into a shared map, much like a mental number line, “Valerio told Earth.com.

“This map brings whole numbers, such as 1 and 2, and fractions, such as 1/2 and 2/3, into the same system, according to their values.”.

The size map demonstrated up in only 14 or 15 of the 20 participants, depending on the number type. The fractions also stopped at 5/2, short of the range the whole numbers covered.

Fractions and whole numbers were mixed in one stream, so people may have had to build a single line to keep up.

It has been revealed that the authors wrote that if the two kinds had been shown in separate sessions, each might still have run from small to large. The two lines might not have lined up, though.

Sources indicate that valério said the study was not designed to explain why fractions are harder to learn or to find the best way to teach them. Other studies in her lab are working on that.

Her next step is to see how the shared map differs across people with different mathematical backgrounds and levels of education, and whether those differences go with mathematical ability.

How the brain represents fractions in children who are still learning them remains an open question.

It has been revealed that the team has posted its data and code on the Open Science Framework. It wrote that longer scanning sessions could extend the map to more kinds of math.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Biology.

It got closer than other robot vacuums we tested, but this is still a common struggle for many other models.

Industry observers note that if you don’t need a robot vacuum with mopping capability, then the Shark PowerDetect is a viable option. It doesn’t sacrifice on features where you need them, and works well on different types of flooring.

Industry observers note that our tester found that the robot vacuum could clean various floor types and pick up after pets with ease. After after just one cycle, they noticed the difference.

In a recent development, the vacuum has one side brush, but since it rotates 360-degrees, it’s able to get close to baseboards and edges without leaving much of anything behind. The PowerDetect also does a great job of moving around obstacles. During testing, the vacuum got pretty close to a hair dryer cord to clean as much of the floor/carpet as possible, but it never tried to vacuum over it or got tangled.

Recent findings suggest that battery life held up too, and the robot vacuum was able to clean multiple rooms before returning to the docking station to charge. Our tester did note that the battery drains faster in Matrix Clean mode, but this isn’t completely unexpected because max suction requires more power.

One of the first things that sets the Eufy Omni S2 is its unique docking station. Most robot vacuums on the market have tanks that are side by side and sit lower to the ground, but the S2’s docking station is taller and more narrow, making it easier to access to refill and empty (and find a place to store).

Industry observers note that another is suction power. The Omni S2 pulls at up to 30,000 Pa, and our tester noticed the difference immediately, especially in high-traffic spots that get flattened and dull over time. The 100 air watts of consistent airflow was able to pull in dirt, allergens, and pet hair from deep between carpet fibers instead of just picking up debris from the surface.

The S2 uses a DuoSpiral main brush, which is actually two separate brush rolls with a gap in the middle to funnel hair into the suction port to prevent tangles, and it has proven reliable in a household with six pets.

Recent findings suggest that most mopping robot vacuums use spinning mop heads to clean your floors, but the Omni S2 uses a rolling mop with electrolyzed water and plenty of downward pressure for an even clean. The main downside is there is no option for mopping-only or vacuum-then-mopping cleaning modes. Many of our other recommendations are able to do these processes separately, so it’s definitely something to consider. The base station takes care of much of the dirty maintenance work, including self-emptying, self-refilling, hot water washing and hot air drying of the mop roller.

Full Eufy Omni S2 Robot Vacuum and Mop Review.

Industry observers note that many robot vacuums overlap in features and capability, and there are newer and better models releasing all the time. As a result, we’re often adding and swapping out our recommendations in this list. Here are a few other robot vacuums we’ve tested that still warrant recognition:.

Eufy X10 Pro Omni Robot Vacuum and Mop: This combination robot vacuum and mop reduces monotonous upkeep tasks with carefully curated features. The docking station lasts for up to 60 days before needing attention, and other key highlights include auto-refill, auto-wash, self-dry, and self-emptying to make maintenance virtually hands-free.

Industry observers note that roborock Curv Flow 2 Robot Vacuum and Mop: The Roborock CurvX we recommend above is the stronger all-around robot vacuum, but the Curv Flow 2 is a good alternative if you want a mop roller that continuously refreshes itself with clean water to prevent dirty mop drag. This robot vacuum is also rated for up to 20,000Pa of suction power, has a larger dustbin, and performs well on hard floors.

Navigation is key to how well a robot vacuum performs its job. Suction matters little if the vacuum fails to cover every part of your floor. Just about all models utilize three fundamental types of sensors to help them navigate.

Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR).

This navigation method involves a laser that locates features by sending out pulses of light and measuring how long they take to return. LiDAR is especially useful for creating accurate maps and is the most powerful and most common navigation tool for robot vacuums.

It has been revealed that with this navigation style, the vacuum travels in one direction and then changes course when it hits an object. A lot of models are programmed to optimize their paths and make them more efficient. By running into a wall in a couple of places, the robot vac can verify the location of the wall and move parallel to it, turning 180 degrees each time they hit an end wall.

Visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (vSLAM).

Industry observers note that this triangulates position by tracking multiple points in a room in successive camera frames. Over time, the vacuum learns and becomes more efficient by relying on points that remain constant and do not change.

Suction power, which indicates how strongly a vacuum pulls in air and debris, is typically listed by the manufacturer in pascals (Pa). The bulk of modern vacuums offer anywhere from 4,000 to 10,000 Pa, but with each latest model that comes out, we’re seeing those numbers continue to rise, with some upwards of 20,000 Pa. Just be aware that higher suction impacts a robot vacuum’s battery life and noise levels.

A brand’s claims about suction power may not provide the full picture, either. Manufacturers don’t tell us exactly where or how they’re measuring—they may take measurements at the impeller or without passing the filter, or using the vacuum only in a controlled environment. It’s similar to how automakers disclose horsepower ratings on cars as an engine spec. The transmission, differential, and other components all leech some of that horsepower, so what’s actually available at the rear wheels differs from the number listed in the specs.

In a recent development, A large dustbin and water tank capacity are ideal for massive homes or households with pets, since they reduce how often you need to empty or refill. For smaller spaces or light daily cleaning, a more compact unit with a capacity of 2 liters should still get the job done. For models that also mop, a clean and dirty water tank of 4 liters or more combined is sufficient for cleaning larger areas efficiently without constant refilling. The models on our list hold between 2.5 and 5.3 liters of debris.

Sources indicate that beyond navigation and suction power, today’s robot vacuums come packed with bells and whistles that elevate them beyond the basic models of the past. Room mapping, self-emptying dustbins, voice assistant compatibility, cleaning schedules, and no-go zones have all become more or less the standard.

It has been revealed that the most tech-forward robot vacuums offer AI-powered obstacle recognition that identifies and steers clear of pet waste, shoes, or cables. There are also variations that have dual functionality, combining both vacuum and mopping qualities. As you might expect, the more advanced sensors and assets a robot vacuum offers, the higher its price tag.

Throughout our testing process, we discovered that while the mopping features are certainly useful, they don’t fully deliver the type of power or pressure needed to get rid of tough stains or set-in messes. The docking stations are also made for water only, and it’s not recommended to use any kind of detergents or DIY solutions in the robot. Some brands make their own cleaners that you can purchase separately, but make sure its compatible with your specific model. If you’re dealing with really stubborn grime, we recommend keeping a standard mop on hand.

Recent findings suggest that look out for shoelaces, string, carpet fringe, and thin or lightweight clothing—all of which gets easily caught in brushes and rollers. Some units have sensors that stop them when the brushes meet resistance, and some move in reverse, spitting out whatever they pulled in. This technology isn’t foolproof, so it’s best to just keep the area clear.

Additionally, be aware of pet bowls, plant stands, or other things that could tip over until you know how the robot vacuum interacts with them. Models that leverage bump-and-go navigation may knock things a little harder, so it’s a good idea to set up boundaries to avoid those obstacles.

Industry observers note that lastly, if you have kids, many robot vacuums are capable of picking up small toys (or parts of toys) that are strewn about. A lot of units have the ability to create exclusion zones, so make use of them, or employ your own strategy to avoid all these little hazards that could jam up the vacuum.

Most homes have places where a robot won’t reach, like in between narrowly spaced furniture legs or tight corners. Also, some types of dirt and debris overwhelm robot vacuum filters, since their capacities are pretty small. Fine dust, fireplace ash, and powders, even in moderate quantities, could clog a filter and affect performance.

Sources indicate that when set on a consistent schedule, robot vacuums help your house look clean on a day-to-day basis. Still, it’s best to run your upright or cordless stick vacuum for deeper cleans and bigger messes.

Industry observers note that place the robot vacuum and docking station in an open space that’s close to a power outlet. The power connection is essential for charging the vacuum and running automatic dustbin emptying features. When the space in front of the docking station is open and obstacle-free, the vacuum is able to tackle dirt more frequently. Try to avoid putting the unit near high-pile carpeting, near stairs, or cluttered spaces.

Industry observers note that for homes with high foot traffic, pets, or children, running your vacuum on a daily basis is ideal. Three to four times a week is best for homes with moderate foot traffic, and if you live in an apartment, or your home has multiple spare rooms that don’t get used very often, running your robot vacuum weekly (or simply as needed) will suffice.

Recent findings suggest that most units have physical controls on the vacuum to start, stop, and send the vacuum back to the docking station. However, smart features like app control, scheduling, mapping, and voice assistants require internet connection. We recommend connecting the vacuum to your home network to get the most out of these features.

Hawaii’s 90-foot Hōlei Sea Arch was carved from lava that flowed about 550 years ago, and in late September it fell into the Pacific

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the 90-foot Hōlei Sea Arch in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park collapsed in late September 2026.
  • For years, visitors who drove to the end of Chain of Craters Road in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park could walk a short distance and see a 90-foot arch of lava rock reaching out from the cliffs into the Pacific Ocean.
  • The Hōlei Sea Arch was still standing on Wednesday, September 23, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the 90-foot Hōlei Sea Arch in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park collapsed in late September 2026. Here is how it formed and why sea arches eventually fall.

For years, visitors who drove to the end of Chain of Craters Road in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park could walk a short distance and see a 90-foot arch of lava rock reaching out from the cliffs into the Pacific Ocean.

That view is gone. The Hōlei Sea Arch was still standing on Wednesday, September 23, 2026. By the night of Sunday, September 27, it had collapsed into the ocean, the National Park Service declared on October 1.

Recent findings suggest that the exact time of the collapse is unknown. According to the park, it could have happened while the park was temporarily closed during Tropical Storm Nolo.

The arch stood about 90 feet (27.4 meters) high and extended from steep sea cliffs into the ocean along the park’s southern coast, on the Island of Hawaiʻi.

Sources indicate that it was carved into the cliff of an ancient lava flow from about 550 years ago, according to the park. The arch took shape through what geologists call differential erosion: some layers of lava are harder than others, so the sea wears them away at different speeds.

Visitors could see it by walking a short distance from the end of Chain of Craters Road, which the park described in 2020 as a 19-mile drive through some of the most spectacular scenery in the park.

Sources indicate that the park’s own page on the arch was clear about one thing. The formation was beautiful but temporary, with a limited life span, and it would eventually crumble into the sea.

Sea arches like Hōlei can be found along a wide stretch of Hawaiʻi’s southern coast. They are remnants of once-continuous sea cliffs, built where lava met the sea and added to the size of the island.

Lava meeting the sea can even build whole new land, as it did when a new island rose from the sea off Iceland in 1963.

It has been revealed that the moment that fresh lava cooled and turned to rock, it began to erode, the park explains. The seas on the island’s southern edge are known for rough water and violent surf, and the waves slowly break apart the rock and carve sea caves into the cliffs.

When waves hit the back wall of a sea cave, the water bounces back and starts to erode the cave’s headland. Over time, that forms an arch.

Sources indicate that the erosion does not stop there. Given enough time, the waves cause the remaining bridge of rock to collapse, leaving behind a pile of rocks known as a sea stack.

Volcanic coastlines are constantly being remade, and on the same island, Kīlauea has produced 55 lava fountains since December 2024.

The coastline around the arch had shown signs of instability for years.

Sources indicate that earthquakes during the 2018 Kīlauea eruption and summit collapse damaged the cliffs near the arch. In January 2020, upcoming cracks and instability led the park to close the original viewing area and the short trail to it.

“This new development reminds us that Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park is an ever-changing volcanic landscape,” Rhonda Loh, then the park’s acting superintendent, noted in January 2020.

A safer viewing area opened in March 2020, about 1,000 feet past the gate at the end of Chain of Craters Road and set back from the cliff edge.

Later that year, massive surf from Tropical Storm Darby broke off a chunk of rock from the lower part of the arch.

The park is urging visitors to stay back from the unstable cliffs, which drop vertically into the ocean and present a serious risk of falling.

After the collapse, photos on social media demonstrated people entering the closed area near where the arch once stood.

According to the park, that puts both the visitors and first responders at great risk of falling and drowning off the rough, wave-swept coast.

Visitors are required to stay out of closed areas and away from cliff edges, which can collapse without warning.

The park describes individual sea arches as an ephemeral feature of the island’s constantly shifting coastline.

As the cliff slowly migrates inland, other arches will form and replace Hōlei, the park says. The park notes that erosion does not stop once an arch has formed.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service’s announcement of the collapse, its pages on Hōlei Sea Arch and how sea arches form, and its 2020 releases on the closure of the overlook and the fresh viewing area.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sebnem Ece Eksi did a double take. Proteins typically studied in the brain were turning up in prostate cancer cells from high-risk patients. These proteins, called neuronal adhesion molecules, play a key role in the circuitry associated with memory.

According to recent reports, the finding, made during her Ph.D. days at the University of Illinois Chicago, raised so many questions to which Eksi is still seeking answers. Now at the Oregon Health & Science University in Portland, Eksi has made it her lab’s goal to find out how nervous systems communicate with cancer. What were once two separate fields might be connected more closely than previously thought.

“What we’re learning is that tumors are actively communicating with the nervous system,” Eksi notes. “In a way, it makes sense to me that a growing tumor in our bodies, in an organ, would be immediately sensed and detected by the nervous system.”.

In a recent development, eksi now intends to test an AI image-based recognition algorithm to identify nerve fibers in human patients. This is exciting, she says, because these nerves aren’t normally visible in patient tumors. But through biopsies, she hopes to map out and observe how the nervous system — which impacts sleep, cognition and pain — changes as cancer progresses. The implications are significant, she says. Could experts use the nervous system to detect cancer early? Can they improve patients’ quality of life?

It has been revealed that “This field of cancer neuroscience can change all different stages of cancer diagnosis and treatments,” Eksi claims. “It’s growing so quickly, the field itself.”.

It has been revealed that the red-hued 4th District, which spreads across eastern Colorado, was unexpectedly competitive this year, a sign of how deep into red turf Democrats were able to compete this year. Boebert had Donald Trump’s endorsement, but her relationship with the president has been strained at times after she began pressing for the release of files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Laubacher proved to be a strong fundraiser, hauling in $13.7 million as of mid-October to Boebert’s $1.2 million.

Boebert has been one of the most visible and controversial members of the House GOP conference since she won an upset primary in the 3rd District over five-term incumbent Republican Scott Tipton in 2020.

It has been revealed that A newcomer to electoral politics, she rapidly positioned herself as a disruptor on Capitol Hill, heckling former President Joe Biden during his 2022 State of the Union address and tangling with a fellow GOP firebrand, former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia, on the House floor.

It has been revealed that in 2023, Boebert was embroiled in an embarrassing incident in a Denver theater that was captured on surveillance video. She subsequently embarked on an apology tour.

Running for reelection the first time in the 3rd District, which is centered around Colorado’s rural Western Slope, Boebert barely won a closer-than-expected race against Democrat Adam Frisch in 2022. When Frisch declared he was trying again in 2024, Boebert switched to the 4th District, which had been considered far friendlier terrain for the GOP.

Sources indicate that this year, Democrats won all of Colorado’s House seats, except in the 3rd District, which is held by Rep. Jeff Hurd.

What satellites leave behind

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • It was early 2023, in Fairbanks, Alaska, in the deep blue of winter, and Murphy and his colleagues had just sent a plane through the stratosphere, the atmospheric stratum 6 to 31 miles (10 to 50 kilometers) above Earth’s surface where the protective ozone layer lies.
  • Their experiment came as interest was growing in controversial proposals to cool the planet by injecting certain aerosols into the atmosphere — a form of geoengineering.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was the lithium that gave it away, states Daniel Murphy, an atmospheric chemist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

It was early 2023, in Fairbanks, Alaska, in the deep blue of winter, and Murphy and his colleagues had just sent a plane through the stratosphere, the atmospheric stratum 6 to 31 miles (10 to 50 kilometers) above Earth’s surface where the protective ozone layer lies.

Their experiment came as interest was growing in controversial proposals to cool the planet by injecting certain aerosols into the atmosphere — a form of geoengineering. The team hoped to get a baseline measurement of the chemistry of the upper atmosphere, before any geoengineering experiments altered the hard-to-reach atmospheric layer.

The lithium showed they were too late.

In a recent development, the team expected to find trace amounts of metals naturally deposited by meteoroids, which constantly bombard and burn up in Earth’s atmosphere. But their data highlighted way more lithium in stratospheric particles than is typically present in meteoroids.

It has been revealed that “That’s what led us to the other metals,” Murphy states. Analyzing their samples, they also found higher than expected levels of aluminum, plus significant amounts of other metals like copper and lead that are scarcely found in meteoroids and must have come from some other source. Then there were the more exotic metals like niobium and hafnium, which appeared in their samples in the same ratio as in an alloy used to manufacture rocket engine nozzles.

The data pointed to an obvious culprit: human-made objects such as satellites and spent rocket stages that fall back to Earth from orbit and reenter the atmosphere. On the way down, they wear away and disintegrate under the heat of friction — a process known as ablation.

Later that year in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), Murphy and his colleagues reported that 10% of stratospheric aerosol particles carried metals from spacecraft.

Industry observers note that the number was shocking, but not altogether surprising. Reentries have been rising sharply in recent years as corporations and countries began launching megaconstellations of thousands of satellites, like SpaceX’s Starlink. And all those satellites will inevitably deorbit.

Industry observers note that since Murphy and his colleagues’ 2023 report, it’s become clear that human-made satellites are now dumping more of certain metals into the upper atmosphere than meteoroids naturally do. This influx has raised concerns that the metals might catalyze chemical reactions that destroy ozone, alter cloud formation, or boost or buffer the greenhouse effect.

Researchers say it’s too soon to know for sure if the metals are a serious environmental problem. But megaconstellations are growing faster than our ability to close these knowledge gaps.

At the same time, the uncertainty over whether regulators might have to act presents a significant risk to the space industry, says Martin Ross of the Aerospace Corporation, a research and development nonprofit based in El Segundo, California, and a co-author of the 2023 study. “We would call it an enterprise risk,” says Ross, “in that the longer we wait to see if there is something going on, the bigger the mitigation will be — if there needs to be any mitigation — down the line.”.

From our vantage point on Earth, space may be incomprehensibly vast, but the orbital environment is not.

Recent findings suggest that six years ago, according to the U.S. Space Force’s public catalog, there were some 13,700 trackable objects circling in low Earth orbit; last year, the number had climbed to nearly 25,000. Disposing of satellites in the atmosphere reduces overcrowding and the risk of uncontrolled objects crashing into each other — and potentially setting off a chain of collisions that wipe out key space-based technologies or turn Earth orbit into an impenetrable debris field.

RELATED: Our increasingly cluttered skies.

According to recent reports, “Reentry is the only sustainable, short-term way of cleaning up the orbital environment,” claims José Pedro Ferreira, a doctoral candidate in astronautical engineering at the University of Southern California (USC) in Los Angeles, who left an industry job for academia in the early 2020s when it became clear that reentry could have unintended consequences. “We need to do it, otherwise we may undermine our capability of accessing orbit.”.

But operators are also typically held responsible by their national regulators for any damages their spacecraft cause on the ground, and for decades the industry has designed spacecraft to burn up as much as possible in the atmosphere to minimize the risk to lives and infrastructure on the ground, a principle known as design for demise.

As a result, the space industry has long perceived its impacts to Earth as minimal. But in the age of megaconstellations, that’s no longer the case.

“As with everything, we live in a closed system,” claims Ferreira, “and things do not disappear.”.

Industry observers note that spaceX launched its first 60 satellites into orbit in May 2019 to bring internet to even remote regions of the globe; less than a decade later, Starlink’s constellation is more than 10,000 satellites strong. Starlink already comprises roughly two-thirds of active satellites, and SpaceX plans to grow it to as many as 42,000. Other countries and corporations are not far behind: Amazon Leo is authorized by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to operate roughly 7,700 satellites; China has plans to deploy some 28,000.

Not only are we launching more than ever, but we’re also bringing spacecraft back down faster than ever before.

In a recent development, for decades, spacecraft have been designed to burn up as much as possible upon reentry to minimize risks to those on the ground. As a result, the space industry has long perceived its impacts to Earth as minimal. But in the age of megaconstellations, that’s no longer the case.

Historically, satellite operators had what Ferreira calls a “gentleman’s agreement” to deorbit their spacecraft within 25 years of mission termination to prevent orbital clutter. Recently, some national authorities have begun enforcing even tighter timelines. The FCC, for example, now enforces a five-year window.

“If you have 50,000 satellites in orbit, which is almost surely going to be reached in the not too distant future, with a design lifetime of five years,” Murphy says, “that would mean a satellite would be reentering and burning up in the atmosphere on average more than once an hour.”.

Industry observers note that operators of megaconstellations may use even shorter timelines for deorbiting satellites, according to Ferreira, bringing them down at the first sign of malfunction. “Which is great from a standpoint of orbital sustainability,” he indicates, “but it starts raising the question more and more about what the impacts are in the atmosphere.”.

There are reasons to be concerned.

It has been revealed that aluminum, for example, which makes up the bulk of most spacecraft, may form aluminum oxides as it breaks down during ablation, which can kick-start a chain of chemical reactions that eat away at ozone, Earth’s main shield against UV radiation. Some atmospheric models suggest that metals from spacecraft in stratospheric particles could seed polar stratospheric clouds, further accelerating ozone depletion.

According to recent reports, injecting aluminum into the upper atmosphere is also the basis of many controversial geoengineering intends. Aluminum compounds would block radiation from the Sun, which could cool down our warming planet. But they might also entrap radiation reflected off the surface of the ocean, which could increase surface temperatures. Opposition to geoengineering has so far stymied any field experiments, but with the number of reentries rising from a few hundred to many thousands per year, an uncontrolled geoengineering experiment on a grand scale may have already begun.

Industry observers note that “The metals are at the same altitude range as the ozone layer, so we have to be concerned about what they would do,” Murphy claims. “We don’t know it’s bad, but we don’t know it isn’t bad either.”.

One reason it’s so difficult to predict the impacts of ablation is that we don’t yet understand what happens to spacecraft during ablation. “We reenter things all the time and we have been since the moment we started launching spacecraft,” says Stijn Lemmens, a space debris mitigation analyst at the European Space Agency (ESA). “It’s fascinating, for something which is so ubiquitous, how little we actually know about it, and how little we used to care about it.”.

Operators have long been incentivized to design spacecraft to burn up as much as possible in the atmosphere, and decades of this design for demise ethos has given the space industry a solid idea of how much material — or how little — will make it to the ground when objects burn through the atmosphere.

Sources indicate that but in terms of that material that is ablated, “we’re really in the dark,” notes Ross. Previous studies have suggested that around 90% of the bodies of orbiting satellites and spent upper stages could be vaporized, later condensing into the nanosized particles the team detected. But, says Ross, “we really don’t understand how these vehicles melt, how they break apart, how they form smoke trails.”.

To quantify the impacts on the atmosphere, researchers start with atmospheric models and then add ablated material, examining how those particles interact with the natural stratospheric background via complex chemical reactions and physical processes like mixing. But the outputs of the atmospheric models are presently held back by our limited understanding of the fiery, complex process of ablation — details like what compounds are being emitted and what size particles are being formed. “We’re basically guessing at this point,” Ross states. “And we’re getting to the limit of what we can do with guessing.”.

To do better, scientists are developing new models of the physics and chemistry of ablation itself. At USC, Ferreira and his colleagues model how ablation produces aluminum oxides in the upper atmosphere, providing atmospheric researchers with inputs for both emissions and particle size. In a 2024 study in Geophysical Research Letters, the team reported that a 550-pound (250 kilograms) satellite — about the size of your average megaconstellation satellite — could deposit some 66 pounds (30 kg) of aluminum oxide nanoparticles in the upper atmosphere. Such particles could remain aloft for upwards of 30 years, potentially catalyzing ozone-destroying reactions as they settle throughout the stratosphere for decades after reentry.

In a recent development, but state-of-the-art ablation models don’t always agree on what products are being formed, according to Ross. A model from researchers at the University of Leeds in the U.K. suggests that aluminum hydroxide, rather than aluminum oxide, may be the main byproduct.

Industry observers note that to validate ablation models and get more useful data from atmospheric models, we need more measurements from reentries. How an object breaks apart as it tumbles through the air is a messy process — a product of astrophysics, fluid mechanics, materials science, and engineering. “You cannot reproduce it on Earth,” Lemmens states. “There is no facility large enough to, in one assessment, combine all the effects.”.

That means scientists need to measure ablation where it’s actually taking place — “take instruments and put them on airplanes and go out and watch these things reenter,” Ross says.

Since the beginning of the Space Age, these kinds of measurements have only been taken a handful of times. Observing space objects from an airplane as they streak through the atmosphere is difficult work — and potentially dangerous. Most reentering objects are uncontrolled, making it hard to predict exactly where the object will hit the atmosphere and how much of it will burn up in the process. Researchers need a degree of certainty to avoid sending a plane full of scientists and sensors up into a debris field. “These types of reentries, which are destructive and still predictable so that you can get close, are extremely rare,” Lemmens notes.

Industry observers note that but in 2024, ESA got lucky. The first of four Cluster II satellites — launched in 2000 to study Earth’s magnetosphere — was poised to reenter the atmosphere, and the agency had a pretty good idea of exactly where and when it would break up over the southern Pacific Ocean.

In a recent development, “We could get close,” Lemmens says. “The drawback is it was in broad daylight, which had not been attempted before on this level of detail.”.

In daytime, the team would have no visual confirmation of reentry, and it would be harder to get clean data than at night. The team had to trust they were pointing their instruments at the right spot, and then look at their data after the fact to see if they caught it. “In the end, it’s a leap of faith,” Lemmens notes. “You predict as well as you can, you fly the plane as well as you can, but in the end, you do it all in the blind,” he says.

Industry observers note that on Sept. 8, a team of scientists took off from Easter Island on a modified Dassault Falcon 900 business jet packed with instruments, and pointed their cameras just above the bright blue horizon roughly 500 miles (800 km) away.

In a recent development, the team used spectroscopic instruments to identify which vapors were coming from the ablating satellite. Since the team knew the material makeup of the satellite, they could gauge its surface temperatures during reentry, as the appearance of specific ions would indicate a certain material had reached its melting point.

According to recent reports, altogether, they captured about 20 seconds of the reentry. Two more satellites from the same cluster were set to reenter within 24 hours of each other on Aug. 31 and Sept. 1, 2026, giving ESA another opportunity to capture more of the reentry process and to fully reconstruct the breakup.

For researchers, one upside to the rapid and unmitigated increase in satellite reentries is more opportunities to capture the process in action.

Some of the best data yet to come will be collected by ESA’s Draco mission, in which the agency plans to build and launch a satellite with the “sole purpose of falling apart again,” indicates Lemmens. Draco will launch in 2027 with an indestructible capsule that will survive reentry, protecting the data collected from the surface of the satellite as it’s torn apart by the atmosphere.

Researchers will be able to combine these onboard data with remote observations, using them to improve or validate existing models of ablation. “That means we, for the first time, will actually have the full story without any ambiguities,” Lemmens indicates.

Once a scientific consensus is reached, then mitigation measures, whether technological or regulatory, can be deployed.

If research confirms that one material or another in spacecraft is particularly damaging to the atmosphere, for example, space operators can remove and replace it. “That was the basis of the success of the Montreal Protocol,” says Ross.

In a recent development, after scientists discovered a hole in the ozone layer in the 1980s, every country in the world signed on to the Montreal Protocol, an international agreement to control the ozone-depleting substances humans were emitting into the atmosphere. The hole has been shrinking ever since. Signed in 1987, the agreement is widely considered one of the most successful environmental treaties to date. Since then, however, other global climate agreements have not fared as well.

Recent findings suggest that still, many remain optimistic, including Ross. He points to the commercial space industry’s track record of working with regulators and astronomers to reduce space debris and light pollution. “There is some current flowing in those lines,” he says.

RELATED: Can robots save Earth orbit?

According to recent reports, some operators have already expressed a commitment to acting on whatever guidelines come out of research on the atmospheric risks. “The difficulty that I have as a responsible operator is, in this particular case, I don’t know what to do,” Vijay Thakur, a technical authority at French satellite corporation Eutelsat, said at an October 2025 panel at the Secure World Foundation’s 7th Summit for Space Sustainability in Paris. There are clear brightness limits he can follow to mitigate impacts to the astronomical community, he noted, but no such guidelines exist yet for atmospheric impacts.

In a recent development, “I want to put the right technical requirements, for me as the operator customer, onto industry so they can build what I need to operate and take it up and bring it back down without damaging anything from 0 kilometers to the von Kármán line,” Thakur noted, referring to the commonly accepted boundary of outer space at 62 miles high (100 km). “Help.”.

There are some design tweaks currently available that could reduce emissions and help more of each spacecraft survive reentry, including non-ablative heat shields and inflatable aerodynamic decelerators, according to Adam Mitchell, a materials and processes evaluation engineer at ESA.

Industry observers note that of course, the more of a spacecraft that survives reentry, the greater the risk on the ground during uncontrolled reentries — and most reentries are uncontrolled. “There is this balance between sustainability and safety, but when it comes to human safety, there is no compromise at all,” Chris Young, space sustainability senior lead at the U.K. Space Agency, said at the same Secure World Foundation panel. “Design for demise has to take priority.”.

Satellite builders could also consider replacing problematic metals — but that comes with its own trade-offs. In 2024, the world’s first wooden satellite, LignoSat, launched to orbit in a partnership between Kyoto University and Japanese logging firm Sumitomo Forestry. A cube of magnolia wood panels, LignoSat will give researchers insights into how well wood holds up in the space environment, and how cleanly it burns up in the atmosphere. Carbon fiber is another material of interest, according to Ferreira. But these organic materials may release black carbon into the upper atmosphere, which may absorb sunlight or reflect it, depending on the structure the carbon takes.

According to recent reports, ross thinks we can close the remaining knowledge gaps in short order — and that those lessons can be applied almost immediately. “We can do that before the next generation of satellites comes along,” he notes, “but we just need the resources.”.

A cultural revolution is coming for the industry, regardless of what’s discovered about the impacts to the atmosphere. “The one-use, nonrecyclable culture that we have in space, of, ‘We’ll launch something to space with rare Earth minerals that are of limited supply and then burn them all up in the atmosphere after one use,’ that is unsustainable,” stated Young.

Industry observers note that A sustainable future — one that balances both Earth and space sustainability — will involve creating something we haven’t quite nailed yet in our earthbound industries. “We need to move beyond the single-use mindset that right now defines much of spacecraft design and accelerate the transition toward an in-space circular economy,” Mitchell states.

According to recent reports, can we do in space what we’ve failed to do on Earth? Right now, researchers are gathering data as fast as they can, as fast as resourcing allows, to inform models of ablation and atmospheric processes that will eventually be validated by measurements taken during reentry.

Then, equipped with actionable data, we can act.

A one-in-a-million catch in a Fresh York harbor turns out to be a bright yellow burbot

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (663 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fish and Wildlife Service crew caught a rare yellow burbot in Oswego Harbor, Upcoming York.
  • Recent findings suggest that biologists with the U.S.
  • Industry observers note that the agency calls it a one-in-a-million catch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service crew caught a rare yellow burbot in Oswego Harbor, Upcoming York. A genetic condition gave it the color, and it went to Cornell.

Recent findings suggest that biologists with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service were running a routine survey in Oswego Harbor, Upcoming York, on Lake Ontario, in October when they pulled up a fish they did not expect. It was a burbot, and it was bright yellow-orange.

Industry observers note that the agency calls it a one-in-a-million catch. The fish has xanthochromism, a rare condition that gives it a saturated yellow-orange color.

The agency remarked the fish would make even the brightest fall foliage look pale in comparison.

It is also the first burbot ever documented during a fisheries survey in Oswego Harbor, although a few anglers have reported catching them there.

Xanthochromism is caused by a genetic mutation that suppresses normal pigmentation and produces the yellow-orange appearance.

It is considerably less common in wild fish than albinism or melanism, according to the Fish and Wildlife Service. Unusual colors like this have surprised scientists before, as with a bright orange shark.

According to recent reports, the place was a surprise too. Burbot populations in the lake are extremely low, and the species usually lives in deeper, cooler water than what is found inside the harbor.

According to recent reports, the crew was not looking for burbot. It came from the Lower Great Lakes Fish and Wildlife Conservation Office, and it was carrying out an Aquatic Invasive Species survey.

The program watches harbors, rivers and bays of the Great Lakes for invasive species on a watchlist.

Because invaders are often rare when they first arrive, the crews use several methods at once, including electrofishing, fyke nets, gill nets and environmental DNA, or eDNA.

Invaders are an old problem in these waters: the Great Lakes have been under invasion from one species for 70 years.

According to recent reports, most fish caught in these surveys are native species. Catching a rare native fish suggests the program may also detect newly arriving invaders when their numbers are still very low.

The agency summed it up as an effective survey strategy, along with a bit of luck.

The burbot is a native fish of the Great Lakes. It tends to live on the lake bottom, and it is the only cod-like fish species in freshwater, according to a New York Sea Grant fact sheet. The same fact sheet calls it a formidable predator.

In the Great Lakes, sea lamprey predation has been a common factor affecting burbot numbers.

A 2006 study led by U.S. Geological Survey scientists found that burbot abundance in eastern Lake Erie increased significantly between 1987 and 2003.

The researchers, writing in Transactions of the American Fisheries Society, attributed the apparent recovery to effective sea lamprey control.

The same study suggested that a relatively high density of alewives, a small plankton-eating fish, probably held burbot numbers down in Lakes Ontario and Michigan at the time.

When U.S. Geological Survey fisheries biologists who know the species processed the yellow burbot, they noticed it was emaciated and looked to be in poor health.

It has been revealed that because of its condition, and because the reasons the species remains so scarce in the lake are still unexplained, the fish was sent to the Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine for a health analysis. The agency has not reported the results.

The agency states the catch could turn out to be lucky for the species too.

The rare fish may offer valuable insight into the health of burbot populations across the basin, and that could help guide how they are managed.

The information was obtained from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, a Fresh York Sea Grant fact sheet and a U.S. Geological Survey study.
